items.q: Who has the authority to cancel a Sprint?
opts: The Scrum Master, if there are too many impediments.
The Developers, if they cannot meet the Sprint Goal.
The Product Owner, if the Sprint Goal becomes obsolete.
Any member of the Scrum Team.
items.exp: Only the Product Owner has the authority to cancel the Sprint, although they may do so under influence from the stakeholders, the Developers, or the Scrum Master.

items.q: What is the timebox for a Sprint Planning event based on a one-month Sprint?
opts: Timeboxed based on how much work is in the Product Backlog
Until all developers agree on the plan
items.exp: Sprint Planning is timeboxed to a maximum of eight hours for a one-month Sprint. For shorter Sprints, the event is usually shorter.

items.q: Which of the following is NOT an official Scrum Artifact?
items.exp: The three artifacts are the Product Backlog, Sprint Backlog, and Increment. The Sprint Goal is a *commitment* contained within the Sprint Backlog, not a standalone artifact.

items.q: Who creates the Definition of Done?
opts: The Scrum Master, to ensure quality.
The Product Owner, based on stakeholder requirements.
If it is not an organizational standard, the Scrum Team must create a Definition of Done appropriate for the product.
The Developers, because they do the work.
items.exp: If the Definition of Done for an increment is part of the standards of the organization, all Scrum Teams must follow it as a minimum. If it is not an organizational standard, the Scrum Team must create a Definition of Done appropriate for the product.

items.q: What happens if an item in the Sprint Backlog cannot be finished by the end of the Sprint?
opts: The Sprint is extended to allow the Developers to finish the work.
It is presented at the Sprint Review as a 'work in progress'.
It is moved to the next Sprint automatically.
It returns to the Product Backlog.
items.exp: If a Product Backlog item does not meet the Definition of Done, it cannot be released or even presented at the Sprint Review. It returns to the Product Backlog for future consideration.

items.q: During a Sprint, a stakeholder approaches a Developer and asks them to add an urgent, small feature. What should the Developer do?
opts: Add it to the Sprint Backlog and work on it, as Scrum requires agility.
Tell the stakeholder to talk to the Product Owner.
Ask the Scrum Master to block the stakeholder from talking to them.
Complete the work but don't mention it in the Daily Scrum to avoid distracting the team.
items.exp: Those wanting to change the Product Backlog can do so only by trying to convince the Product Owner. The Product Owner is accountable for maximizing the value of the product.

items.q: What is the primary difference between the Sprint Review and the Sprint Retrospective?
opts: The Review inspects the process; the Retrospective inspects the product.
The Review inspects the product; the Retrospective inspects the process (individuals, interactions, tools).
The Review is for management; the Retrospective is for the Scrum Team.
There is no difference; they are two names for the same event.
items.exp: The Sprint Review is to inspect the outcome of the Sprint (the Increment) and determine future adaptations. The Sprint Retrospective is to plan ways to increase quality and effectiveness (process).

items.q: How many Product Owners should there be for a product being built by three separate Scrum Teams?
opts: Three Product Owners, one for each team.
One Product Owner, but they can delegate their responsibilities to a Chief Product Owner.
As many as the teams need to ensure fast decision making.
items.exp: One Product, One Product Backlog, One Product Owner. This remains true regardless of the number of Scrum Teams working on the product.

items.q: Which Scrum Value is demonstrated when a Developer admits they made a mistake that caused the build to fail?
items.exp: Openness: The Scrum Team and its stakeholders agree to be open about all the work and the challenges with performing the work.

items.q: Who determines how work gets done during the Sprint?
items.exp: The Developers are always accountable for creating a plan for the Sprint, the Sprint Backlog. How they turn Product Backlog items into an Increment of value is solely up to them.

items.q: What is the main reason for the Scrum Master to be at the Daily Scrum?
opts: To gather status and progress information.
To write down any changes to the Sprint Backlog.
They do not have to be there; they only need to ensure the Developers have the event.
To make sure every team member answers the three questions.
items.exp: The Daily Scrum is an event for the Developers. The Scrum Master ensures it takes place, but attends as a participant only if they are actively working on items in the Sprint Backlog.

items.q: When many Scrum Teams are working on a single product, what should best describe the Definition of Done?
opts: Each Scrum Team must have a separate Definition of Done.
All Scrum Teams must have a mutually defining Definition of Done that makes their combined work potentially releasable.
items.exp: If there are multiple Scrum Teams working together on a product, they must mutually define and comply with the same Definition of Done.

items.q: Which of the following is true regarding the Product Backlog?
opts: It is managed by the Scrum Master.
It only contains bugs and technical debt.
It is finalized before the first Sprint.
items.exp: The Product Backlog is never complete. The earliest development of it lays out the initially known and best-understood requirements, but it evolves as the product and the environment in which it will be used evolves.

items.q: Who is responsible for managing the progress of work during a Sprint?
items.exp: The Developers are always accountable for creating a plan for the Sprint (Sprint Backlog), instilling quality, and adapting their plan each day toward the Sprint Goal.

items.q: A Scrum Team is working on a 4-week Sprint. How long should their Sprint Review be?
opts: As long as it takes to show all the work
items.exp: The Sprint Review is timeboxed to a maximum of four hours for a one-month Sprint. For shorter Sprints, the event is usually shorter.

items.q: What is the result of the Sprint Review?
opts: A revised Product Backlog that defines the probable Product Backlog items for the next Sprint.
A finalized design for the next Sprint.
items.exp: The Sprint Review includes a discussion of what to do next, so the Product Backlog may also be adjusted to meet new opportunities. The result of the Sprint Review is a revised Product Backlog.

items.q: True or False: The Scrum Master can order the Product Backlog if the Product Owner is too busy.
items.exp: False. The Product Owner may delegate the work of managing the Product Backlog, but they remain accountable. The Scrum Master cannot arbitrarily take over this accountability.

items.q: When can a Sprint be cancelled?
opts: When the Developers feel they cannot finish the work.
When the Scrum Master identifies too many impediments.
If the Sprint Goal becomes obsolete.
A Sprint can never be cancelled.
items.exp: A Sprint could be cancelled if the Sprint Goal becomes obsolete. Only the Product Owner has the authority to cancel the Sprint.

items.q: Which two things does the Scrum framework use to optimize predictability and control risk?
items.exp: Scrum employs an iterative, incremental approach to optimize predictability and to control risk. It is founded on empiricism and lean thinking.

items.q: What does it mean for a Scrum Team to be cross-functional?
opts: Every member of the team must have the same skills.
The team members have all the skills necessary to create value each Sprint.
They can work across different projects simultaneously.
items.exp: Cross-functional teams have all competencies needed to accomplish the work without depending on others not part of the team.

items.q: During Sprint Planning, the Developers realize they have taken on too much work. What should they do?
opts: Collaborate with the Product Owner to remove or change items.
items.exp: If the Developers determine they have too much or too little work, they may renegotiate the selected Product Backlog items with the Product Owner.

items.q: What is the primary way a Scrum Master keeps the Developers working at its highest level of productivity?
opts: By ensuring the meetings start and end at the proper time.
By facilitating Developer decisions and removing impediments.
By keeping track of task hours.
items.exp: The Scrum Master serves the Scrum Team in several ways, including causing the removal of impediments to the Scrum Team's progress and coaching the team members in self-management and cross-functionality.

items.q: Who is responsible for engaging the stakeholders?
items.exp: The Product Owner is accountable for maximizing the value of the product, which includes representing the desires of the stakeholders to the Scrum Team.

items.q: Which statement best describes the Sprint Backlog as an artifact?
opts: It is the Product Owner's plan for the Sprint.
It is a highly visible, real-time picture of the work that the Developers plan to accomplish during the Sprint.
It is a list of tasks that must be completed.
It is a fixed commitment that cannot change.
items.exp: The Sprint Backlog is a plan by and for the Developers. It is a highly visible, real-time picture of the work that the Developers plan to accomplish during the Sprint in order to achieve the Sprint Goal.

items.q: When must the Definition of Done be created?
opts: Before an Increment can be considered Done.
By the end of the first Sprint.
items.exp: If it is not an organizational standard, the Scrum Team must create a Definition of Done appropriate for the product before any Increment can be considered Done.

items.q: True or False: The Scrum Team must choose at least one high priority process improvement item from the Sprint Retrospective and place it in the Sprint Backlog for the next Sprint.
items.exp: False. This was a rule in the 2017 Scrum Guide, but it was removed in the 2020 Scrum Guide to make the framework less prescriptive. It is a good practice, but not mandatory.

items.q: What is the purpose of a Sprint?
opts: To release a new feature to customers.
To produce a Done Increment that meets the Sprint Goal.
To complete all items in the Sprint Backlog.
items.exp: The heart of Scrum is a Sprint, a timebox of one month or less during which a "Done", useable, and potentially releasable product Increment is created.

items.q: Who is accountable for the creation of the Definition of Done?
items.exp: If the Definition of Done for an increment is part of the standards of the organization, all Scrum Teams must follow it. If it is not an organizational standard, the Scrum Team must create a Definition of Done appropriate for the product.

items.q: Which of the following is an accountability of the Scrum Master?
opts: Helping the Scrum Team understand the need for clear and concise Product Backlog items.
Estimating the effort of Product Backlog items.
items.exp: The Scrum Master serves the Product Owner by helping find techniques for effective Product Goal definition and Product Backlog management, and helping the Scrum Team understand the need for clear and concise Product Backlog items.

items.q: When is the Sprint Retrospective held?
opts: After the Sprint Review and prior to the next Sprint Planning.
In the middle of the Sprint.
Whenever the team feels they need to improve.
items.exp: The Sprint Retrospective concludes the Sprint. It is held after the Sprint Review and prior to the next Sprint Planning.

items.q: What does the Scrum Master do if the Developers do not have all the skills necessary to complete the Sprint Backlog?
opts: Facilitate the team in finding a solution (e.g., learning, bringing in an expert temporarily).
Tell the Product Owner to remove the items.
items.exp: The Scrum Master is a coach and facilitator. They help the team self-manage to solve their own problems, such as skill gaps.

items.q: How much time should the Scrum Team allocate to Product Backlog refinement?
opts: As much time as is needed.
It must only happen during Sprint Planning.
items.exp: The 2017 Guide suggested 10%, but the 2020 Guide removed this. Refinement is an ongoing activity to add details, such as a description, order, and size. The Scrum Team decides how and when refinement is done.

items.q: Which Scrum Value is demonstrated by a Developer asking for help when they are stuck?
items.exp: Openness. The Scrum Team and its stakeholders agree to be open about all the work and the challenges with performing the work.

items.q: What is the maximum length of a Sprint?
items.exp: Sprints are fixed length events of one month or less to create consistency.

items.q: Who is permitted to change the Sprint Backlog during a Sprint?
items.exp: The Sprint Backlog is a plan by and for the Developers. Only the Developers can change its contents during a Sprint as they learn more about the work needed to achieve the Sprint Goal.

items.q: If an organization wants to scale Scrum to 3 teams working on one product, how many Definition of Dones should they have?
items.exp: If there are multiple Scrum Teams working together on a product, they must mutually define and comply with the same Definition of Done.

items.q: Who is responsible for sizing (estimating) Product Backlog items?
items.exp: The Developers who will be doing the work are responsible for the sizing. The Product Owner may influence the Developers by helping them understand and select trade-offs.

items.q: Which event provides an opportunity to inspect the Increment and adapt the Product Backlog?
items.exp: The purpose of the Sprint Review is to inspect the outcome of the Sprint and determine future adaptations. The Scrum Team presents the results of their work to key stakeholders.

items.q: What is the role of Management in Scrum?
opts: To support the Product Owner with insights and information into high value product and system capabilities, and to support the Scrum Master in causing organizational change.
Management has no role in Scrum.
items.exp: Management supports the Scrum Team by providing resources, strategic direction, and helping remove organizational impediments.

items.q: What does the Agile Manifesto say about 'Responding to change'—
opts: Responding to change over following a plan.
Responding to change over comprehensive documentation.
Responding to change over contract negotiation.
Responding to change over individuals and interactions.
items.exp: The Agile Manifesto values 'Responding to change over following a plan'.

items.q: A Scrum Team completes a Sprint but skips the Sprint Retrospective because 'the Sprint went well and there's nothing to improve.' Which pillar of empiricism does this violate?
items.exp: Adaptation is adjusting the process based on what inspection reveals. Skipping the Retrospective removes the team's only formal opportunity to adapt how it works — even a smooth Sprint has room for it, since 'nothing to improve' is itself a conclusion that requires inspection to reach.

items.q: During a Sprint, a Developer notices they are struggling to finish their work and, instead of hiding it, immediately raises it at the Daily Scrum so the team can re-plan. Which Scrum Value is being demonstrated?
items.exp: Openness is the Scrum Team and its stakeholders agreeing to be open about the work and the challenges. Surfacing a struggle immediately, rather than concealing it, is openness in action.

items.q: According to the Scrum Guide, what is Scrum?
opts: A prescriptive methodology that defines every process, technique, and tool a team must use
A lightweight framework that helps people generate value through adaptive solutions for complex problems
A software development lifecycle owned and maintained by a single vendor
items.exp: The Scrum Guide explicitly defines Scrum as a lightweight framework, not a methodology or a complete product — it deliberately leaves room for teams to implement other practices, techniques, and methods within it.

items.q: The Product Owner is unreachable for two days during a Sprint, and the Developers have a question about which of two acceptable implementations best serves an item's intent. What should the Developers do?
opts: Halt all work until the Product Owner responds
Use their best judgment based on the Product Backlog item's existing detail and continue, flagging the decision for the Product Owner later
Let the Scrum Master make the final call permanently
items.exp: The Product Owner remains accountable for the Product Backlog, but Developers are trusted to interpret existing detail and keep moving — that's what 'self-managing' means. A two-day gap isn't grounds to halt the Sprint or permanently hand the decision to someone else.

items.q: What does the 2020 Scrum Guide say about the size of a Scrum Team?
opts: Usually 10 or fewer, small enough to remain nimble and large enough to complete significant work within a Sprint
As many as the Product Owner decides is necessary
There is no guidance on team size
items.exp: The Scrum Guide says the Scrum Team is typically 10 or fewer people: small enough to remain nimble and large enough to complete significant work within a Sprint.

items.q: Which of the following is something the Scrum Master does specifically to serve the Product Owner?
opts: Estimating Product Backlog items on the Product Owner's behalf
Helping find techniques for effective Product Goal definition and Product Backlog management
Making the final call on which items are prioritized
Attending the Daily Scrum as a required participant every day
items.exp: The Scrum Master serves the Product Owner by helping find techniques for effective Product Goal definition and Product Backlog management — not by estimating, prioritizing, or attending the Daily Scrum by default.

items.q: A Scrum Master notices the wider organization still runs annual budgeting cycles that conflict with the team's ability to adapt quickly. What is the Scrum Master's responsibility here?
opts: Ignore it — organizational process is outside Scrum's scope
Lead the organization in adopting Scrum, helping employees and stakeholders understand and enact an empirical approach
Escalate to the Product Owner to resolve alone
Wait until a Developer raises it at a Retrospective
items.exp: Serving the organization is an explicit Scrum Master accountability — leading, training, and coaching the organization in its Scrum adoption, including working to remove barriers like conflicting processes.

items.q: What does it mean for the Developers to be 'self-managing,' per the 2020 Scrum Guide?
opts: They choose who works on what, when, and how, within the Sprint
They report to a project manager who assigns daily tasks
The Scrum Master assigns work each morning at the Daily Scrum
The Product Owner decides how the work gets done
items.exp: Self-managing (the 2020 Guide's update from 'self-organizing') specifically means the Developers internally decide who does what, when, and how — no one outside the team, including the Scrum Master or Product Owner, assigns that work.

items.q: Who is required to attend the Daily Scrum?
opts: The entire Scrum Team, including the Product Owner and Scrum Master, every day
Only the Developers; the Product Owner or Scrum Master attend only if they are actively working on Sprint Backlog items
Only the Scrum Master, who then reports status to the Developers
Whichever stakeholders are available that day
items.exp: The Daily Scrum is for the Developers. The Product Owner or Scrum Master participate only when they are actively working on items in the Sprint Backlog — otherwise they are not required attendees.

items.q: What is the timebox for the Daily Scrum, regardless of Sprint length?
opts: 30 minutes, matching the Sprint Review's minimum
1 hour per week of Sprint length
There is no fixed timebox — it ends when the team feels done
items.exp: The Daily Scrum is always timeboxed to 15 minutes, no matter how long the Sprint is — unlike Sprint Planning, Review, and Retrospective, which scale with Sprint length.

items.q: Sprint Planning addresses three topics. Which of the following is NOT one of them?
opts: What can be Done this Sprint?
How will the chosen work get done?
Who on the team will be promoted this quarter?
items.exp: Sprint Planning covers Why (the Sprint's value/Sprint Goal), What (which Product Backlog items), and How (the plan to deliver them) — team member promotions have nothing to do with the event.

items.q: During the Daily Scrum, the Developers realize the current plan will not achieve the Sprint Goal without changes. What should happen?
opts: The Developers adjust the Sprint Backlog as necessary, re-planning the remaining work with the Product Owner as needed
Nothing — the Sprint Backlog is fixed once Sprint Planning ends
The Scrum Master rewrites the Sprint Backlog alone
items.exp: The Sprint Backlog is a highly visible, real-time picture of the work Developers plan to accomplish — it's expected to be updated throughout the Sprint as new information emerges, including at or because of the Daily Scrum.

items.q: A Scrum Team had a smooth Sprint with no major issues and considers skipping the Sprint Retrospective to save time. Is this acceptable per the Scrum Guide?
opts: Yes, if the Product Owner approves skipping it
No — the Sprint Retrospective concludes the Sprint and must always be held
Yes, retrospectives are optional if the team is experienced
No, but only if the Sprint Goal was not met
items.exp: The Sprint Retrospective is a required event that concludes every Sprint — it's never optional, regardless of how smoothly the Sprint went, because inspecting and adapting the team's own process is an ongoing, not conditional, practice.

items.q: Once a Sprint has started, can its planned duration be shortened or lengthened?
opts: Yes, at any time, by the Scrum Master
No — the Sprint's duration is fixed once it begins; only the Product Owner can end it early by cancelling it
Yes, if the Developers vote unanimously
Yes, but only by extending it, never shortening it
items.exp: A Sprint's length is fixed for its duration once it starts. The only way to end it early is Sprint cancellation, which only the Product Owner can invoke — there's no mechanism to simply shorten or extend an in-progress Sprint.

items.q: Can a new Sprint begin before the current one officially ends?
opts: Yes, Sprints can overlap to save time
No — a new Sprint starts immediately upon the conclusion of the previous Sprint
Yes, if the Sprint Goal was already achieved early
items.exp: The Scrum Guide is explicit: a new Sprint starts immediately after the conclusion of the previous Sprint. There is no gap between Sprints and no overlap.

items.q: Each of Scrum's three artifacts has an associated commitment. Which pairing is correct?
items.exp: The correct pairings are: Product Backlog → Product Goal, Sprint Backlog → Sprint Goal, Increment → Definition of Done. Sprint Backlog's commitment is the Sprint Goal.

items.q: Can more than one Increment be created within a single Sprint?
opts: No, exactly one Increment is created per Sprint
Yes — multiple Increments can be created within a Sprint, and the sum is presented at Sprint Review
Only if the Sprint length exceeds two weeks
Increments are only created at the very end of the Sprint
items.exp: Multiple Increments may be created within a Sprint as work is completed and verified against the Definition of Done — the cumulative work forms the current Increment, which is inspected at Sprint Review.

items.q: Who is responsible for Product Backlog refinement?
opts: Only the Product Owner, working alone
A collaborative activity between the Product Owner and the Developers, done as an ongoing process rather than a dedicated formal event
The Scrum Master, as one of their core accountabilities
It happens automatically during Sprint Planning only
items.exp: Refinement is the act of breaking down and further defining Product Backlog items into smaller, more precise items — it's an ongoing activity, collaborative between the Product Owner and Developers, and is explicitly NOT one of the formal Scrum events.

items.q: What must be true of an Increment before it can be considered part of a potentially releasable set of Increments?
opts: It must be deployed to production immediately
It must meet the Definition of Done
It must be personally approved by the Scrum Master
It must include at least three Product Backlog items
items.exp: An Increment is only usable, and only counts, once it meets the Definition of Done — the shared, formal description of what 'complete' means for the work, regardless of whether it's actually deployed.

items.q: A single product is being built by three Scrum Teams. How many Product Backlogs should exist?
opts: Three — one per team, tracked independently
One — a single Product Backlog for the entire product, even when multiple teams work on it
One per feature area, regardless of team count
It depends on how the Product Owner wants to organize the work
items.exp: There is only ever one Product Backlog per product, even when multiple Scrum Teams build it together — fragmenting it into per-team backlogs breaks the single, ordered source of truth the framework depends on.

items.q: In Scrum, empiricism asserts that knowledge comes from:
opts: Experience and making decisions based on what is observed
items.exp: Empiricism (the foundation of Scrum) asserts that knowledge comes from experience and making decisions based on what is observed. The three pillars are inspection, adaptation, and transparency.

items.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the three pillars of empirical process control in Scrum?
items.exp: The three pillars are Transparency, Inspection, and Adaptation. While Scrum aims to improve predictability, it is not a foundational pillar itself.

items.q: Scrum is best described as a:
items.exp: Scrum is a lightweight framework that helps people, teams and organizations generate value through adaptive solutions for complex problems. It is not a rigid methodology or process.

items.q: Who is responsible for maximizing the value of the product resulting from the work of the Scrum Team?
items.exp: The Product Owner is accountable for maximizing the value of the product resulting from the work of the Scrum Team, primarily by managing the Product Backlog.

items.q: What is the primary responsibility of the Scrum Master?
opts: Establishing Scrum as defined in the Scrum Guide and coaching the team
items.exp: The Scrum Master is accountable for establishing Scrum as defined in the Scrum Guide. They do this by helping everyone understand Scrum theory and practice, acting as a true leader who serves the Scrum Team.

items.q: Who is responsible for creating the Sprint Backlog?
items.exp: The Developers are always accountable for creating a plan for the Sprint (the Sprint Backlog), instilling quality, and adapting their plan each day toward the Sprint Goal.

items.q: What is the timebox for a Daily Scrum?
opts: Timeboxed to 15 minutes for a one-month Sprint
items.exp: The Daily Scrum is a 15-minute event for the Developers of the Scrum Team, regardless of the Sprint length.

items.q: What is the purpose of the Sprint Review?
opts: To demo the product to the Product Owner for approval
To inspect the outcome of the Sprint and determine future adaptations
To review the team's performance and process
items.exp: The purpose of the Sprint Review is to inspect the outcome of the Sprint and determine future adaptations. The Scrum Team presents the results of their work to key stakeholders and progress toward the Product Goal is discussed.

items.q: When does a Sprint end?
opts: When all Sprint Backlog items are completed
When the Product Owner accepts the increment
items.exp: Sprints are fixed length events of one month or less. A new Sprint starts immediately after the conclusion of the previous Sprint (which ends when its timebox expires).

items.q: What is the commitment for the Product Backlog?
items.exp: Each artifact contains a commitment. For the Product Backlog, the commitment is the Product Goal.

items.q: What is the commitment for the Sprint Backlog?
items.exp: The commitment for the Sprint Backlog is the Sprint Goal, which provides a single objective for the Sprint.

items.q: Which artifact represents a concrete stepping stone toward the Product Goal?
items.exp: An Increment is a concrete stepping stone toward the Product Goal. Each Increment is additive to all prior Increments and thoroughly verified.

items.q: When multiple Scrum Teams are working on the same product, how many Product Backlogs should they have?
opts: It depends on the framework (Nexus vs SAFe)
items.exp: Regardless of the scaling framework, if multiple teams are working on the same product, there is only ONE Product Backlog and ONE Product Owner to ensure a unified vision and prioritization.

items.q: In the Nexus framework, what is the purpose of the Nexus Integration Team?
opts: To do the integration work for the teams
To ensure that a 'Done' Integrated Increment is produced at least every Sprint
To act as a project management office (PMO)
items.exp: The Nexus Integration Team is accountable for ensuring that a 'Done' Integrated Increment (the combined work of all Scrum Teams) is produced at least once a Sprint.

items.q: When scaling Scrum, what is typically the biggest challenge teams face?
items.exp: Managing dependencies between teams and ensuring frequent, successful integration of their code is universally the hardest part of scaling agile development.

items.q: Which of the following is a core practice of Kanban but NOT a mandated rule in Scrum?
items.exp: Kanban relies heavily on explicitly limiting Work in Progress (WIP) to improve flow. Scrum limits WIP implicitly via the Sprint timebox, but does not explicitly require WIP limits on the board.

items.q: A team using 'Scrumban' typically adopts which Kanban element to improve their Scrum flow?
opts: Visualizing flow and applying WIP limits to the Sprint Backlog
items.exp: Scrumban teams keep the Scrum framework (roles, events, artifacts) but apply Kanban practices like visualizing the workflow states (beyond just To Do, Doing, Done) and applying WIP limits to columns.

items.q: In Kanban, what does lead time measure?
opts: The time it takes to write a user story
The time from when a request is made until it is delivered to the customer
The time it takes a developer to code a feature once started
items.exp: Lead time is a key Kanban metric measuring the total time from the customer request to delivery. Cycle time measures the time work is actively being worked on.

items.q: Who has the authority to cancel a Sprint?
items.back: Only the Product Owner.
items.analogy: The Product Owner is the investor who funded the sprint. If market conditions change drastically mid-trade, only the investor can pull the capital — not the traders doing the work.

items.q: Can a Sprint be extended by 2 days if the Developers just need a little more time to finish an item?
items.back: No. Sprints are strict timeboxes. Unfinished items return to the Product Backlog.
items.analogy: A Sprint is a sacred timeboxing contract — like a trading window. When the market closes, it closes. Extending the Sprint would corrupt the empirical cadence Scrum depends on.

items.q: What happens if an item is not "Done" by the end of the Sprint?
items.back: It cannot be presented at the Sprint Review. It returns to the Product Backlog.
items.analogy: Undone work returns to the Product Backlog like a trade order that expired — it doesn't auto-carry over. The Product Owner re-evaluates its priority for the next Sprint based on current conditions.

items.q: Who determines how many Product Backlog items are selected for a Sprint?
items.back: Only the Developers.
items.analogy: Developers are the engineers who know how much they can actually build. Letting the PO or SM dictate capacity is like having the investor tell the quant how many models he can backtest — completely backwards.

items.q: What is the timebox for a Sprint Planning event based on a one-month Sprint?
items.back: Maximum of 8 hours.
items.analogy: Sprint Planning's 8-hour cap enforces discipline — not every detail can be planned upfront. Scrum bets on adaptation over exhaustive upfront planning. Overly long planning sessions signal waterfall thinking.

items.q: What is the timebox for a Daily Scrum?
items.back: 15 minutes for any length of Sprint.
items.analogy: 15 minutes is the Daily Scrum's enforced discipline — it's a sync, not a strategy session. Like a market open briefing: what's the position, what's the risk, what's blocking the trade.

items.q: Who must attend the Daily Scrum?
items.back: The Developers. (PO and Scrum Master only attend if they are actively working on Sprint Backlog items).
items.analogy: The Daily Scrum belongs to the Developers — the people doing the work. The Scrum Master and Product Owner are welcome but not required unless they're also contributing to the Sprint Goal.

items.q: What is the timebox for a Sprint Review based on a one-month Sprint?
items.back: Maximum of 4 hours.
items.analogy: Sprint Review gets 4 hours for a one-month Sprint. It's the investor presentation at the end of a fund cycle — show what was built, get feedback, adjust the roadmap based on reality.

items.q: What is the timebox for a Sprint Retrospective based on a one-month Sprint?
items.back: Maximum of 3 hours.
items.analogy: The Retrospective (3 hrs/month) is the post-trade analysis — what worked, what didn't, what process change would improve the next Sprint's returns. Teams who skip it repeat the same mistakes.

items.q: What is the commitment for the Product Backlog?
items.back: The Product Goal.
items.analogy: The Product Goal is the product's north star — like a fund's investment thesis. Every item in the backlog should trace back to it. It focuses the team on what actually matters.

items.q: What is the commitment for the Sprint Backlog?
items.back: The Sprint Goal.
items.analogy: The Sprint Goal is the tactical objective for this Sprint — like targeting a specific sector for the quarter. It gives the Developers latitude to adapt HOW they achieve it while keeping the outcome fixed.

items.q: What is the commitment for the Increment?
items.back: The Definition of Done.
items.analogy: The Definition of Done is the quality floor — the minimum bar an Increment must clear before it can be shipped. Like a trade that must clear compliance review before it executes.

items.q: Can a Scrum Team have multiple active Product Goals at the same time?
items.back: No. They must fulfill or abandon one Product Goal before taking on the next.
items.analogy: No — multiple Product Goals simultaneously would be like a fund trying to execute two conflicting investment theses at once. Focus is the entire point of the Product Goal commitment.

items.q: Who creates the Definition of Done?
items.back: If it is not an organizational standard, the Scrum Team must create a Definition of Done appropriate for the product.
items.analogy: If no org-wide standard exists, the Scrum Team defines their own DoD. It's their quality contract with themselves — and with the stakeholders who rely on 'Done' meaning something real.

items.q: What are the three pillars of Empiricism?
items.back: Transparency, Inspection, and Adaptation.
items.analogy: Transparency + Inspection + Adaptation = the scientific method applied to product development. You can't inspect what's hidden; you can't adapt if you don't inspect. All three must exist together.

items.q: What are the five Scrum Values?
items.back: Commitment, Focus, Openness, Respect, Courage.
items.analogy: Commitment, Focus, Openness, Respect, Courage — the team culture that makes empiricism safe. Without courage to surface bad news, transparency breaks down. Without respect, no one speaks up.

items.q: Who is accountable for maximizing the value of the product?
items.back: The Product Owner.
items.analogy: The Product Owner is the fund manager — maximizing ROI on the development investment. They order the backlog by value, not by stakeholder politics.

items.q: Who is responsible for all estimates in the Product Backlog?
items.back: The Developers. (The PO may influence them by helping them understand and select trade-offs, but the people who will do the work make the final estimate).
items.analogy: Developers own estimates because they're the ones doing the work. PO setting estimates without developer input would be like a CFO estimating engineering effort — a recipe for missed deadlines.

items.q: When is an Increment born?
items.back: The moment a Product Backlog item meets the Definition of Done.
items.analogy: An Increment is born the moment any Product Backlog item meets the Definition of Done — even mid-Sprint. Increments can be delivered to users at any time; the Sprint Review is just a formal inspection moment.

items.q: Who is accountable for instilling quality by adhering to a Definition of Done?
items.back: The Developers.
items.analogy: Developers own quality — not QA, not the SM. Scrum has no QA team by design. The Definition of Done is the quality gate that every Developer is accountable to.

items.q: What is the purpose of the Daily Scrum?
items.back: To inspect progress toward the Sprint Goal and adapt the Sprint Backlog as necessary.
items.analogy: The Daily Scrum is a 15-minute tactical huddle to inspect progress toward the Sprint Goal and adapt the plan. It is NOT a status meeting for the Scrum Master or PO — it's the Developers' planning tool.

items.q: What happens between the end of one Sprint and the start of the next?
items.back: Nothing. A new Sprint starts immediately after the conclusion of the previous Sprint.
items.analogy: Nothing happens between Sprints — a new Sprint starts immediately on the day the previous one ends. There's no 'Sprint 0' or buffer period. The cadence is continuous and relentless.

items.q: Can the Sprint Goal be changed during the Sprint?
items.back: No. During the Sprint, no changes are made that would endanger the Sprint Goal.
items.analogy: The Sprint Goal is sacred during the Sprint. Changing it would negate the point of the timebox. If the Sprint Goal becomes obsolete, only the Product Owner can cancel the Sprint.

items.q: Who is accountable for establishing Scrum as defined in the Scrum Guide?
items.back: The Scrum Master.
items.analogy: The Scrum Master is accountable for Scrum being understood and enacted correctly — they're the process guardian, not the project manager. Their job is to remove the obstacles that prevent the team from being effective.

items.q: If multiple Scrum Teams are working on the same product, how many Product Backlogs and Product Owners should they have?
items.back: One Product Backlog and One Product Owner.
items.analogy: One Product Backlog, one Product Owner, one Product Goal for multiple teams — like multiple trading desks within one fund all working the same strategy. Each team selects from the same ordered list of priorities.

items.q: What topics are discussed during Sprint Planning?
items.back: Topic 1: Why is this Sprint valuable? Topic 2: What can be Done this Sprint? Topic 3: How will the chosen work get done?
items.analogy: Sprint Planning covers: Why (the Sprint Goal), What (selected PBIs), and How (the plan). Teams that skip 'Why' often build the right features for the wrong reason.

items.q: Does the Scrum Master assign tasks to Developers during the Sprint?
items.back: No. The Developers are self-managing and decide who does what, when, and how.
items.analogy: Scrum Masters don't assign work — Developers self-organize and pull tasks. A SM who assigns work has become a project manager, which undermines the team's ownership and accountability.

items.q: When does the Product Backlog refinement happen?
items.back: It is an ongoing activity. The Scrum Team decides how and when refinement is done.
items.analogy: Refinement is ongoing throughout the Sprint — it's not a single meeting. Think of it as continuous pre-trade research: the team is always sharpening the next set of opportunities.

items.q: Is it mandatory for the Scrum Team to release an Increment to production at the end of every Sprint?
items.back: No. An Increment must be usable and meet the DoD, but the Product Owner decides when to release it.
items.analogy: Releasing is a business decision (PO), not a Scrum requirement. Scrum only requires that the Increment meets DoD and is potentially releasable. Whether to ship is separate from whether it's Done.

items.q: Who is a "true leader who serves"—
items.back: The Scrum Master.
items.analogy: The Scrum Master is a servant-leader — they lead by removing friction, not by directing work. They serve the team, the PO, and the organization by making Scrum effective.

items.q: What is the recommended size of a Scrum Team?
items.back: Small enough to remain nimble and large enough to complete significant work within a Sprint, typically 10 or fewer people.
items.analogy: 10 or fewer is the magic number — small enough to communicate without a meeting, large enough to get real work done. Larger teams create coordination overhead that kills velocity.

items.q: Who comprises the Scrum Team?
items.back: One Scrum Master, one Product Owner, and Developers.
items.analogy: Scrum Team = Developers + Product Owner + Scrum Master. No 'QA team', no 'architects', no 'project managers' — Scrum deliberately collapses those silos into one accountable unit.

items.q: True or False: The Scrum Master must be a technical expert in the product being built.
items.back: False. Their expertise is in the Scrum framework and facilitation, though technical knowledge can be helpful.
items.analogy: False. The Scrum Master masters the Scrum process, not the technology. They help the team remove process obstacles, not debug code. A great SM can serve a hardware team as well as a software team.

items.q: What is the primary difference between the Sprint Review and the Sprint Retrospective?
items.back: Review inspects the PRODUCT (what was built). Retrospective inspects the PROCESS (how it was built).
items.analogy: Sprint Review = inspect the product with stakeholders (external focus). Sprint Retrospective = inspect the process with the team (internal focus). One faces outward, one faces inward.

items.q: If an item in the Sprint Backlog cannot be finished, who must be informed?
items.back: The Product Owner, so scope can be clarified and renegotiated without endangering the Sprint Goal.
items.analogy: Developers own this conversation. They must immediately raise it in the Daily Scrum so the team can adapt — drop scope, renegotiate with PO, or swarm the item. No surprises at the end of the Sprint.

items.q: Who manages the Sprint Backlog?
items.back: Only the Developers.
items.analogy: Developers own and manage the Sprint Backlog. It's their tactical plan, not the SM's task list. The PO can clarify but cannot direct how items are ordered within the Sprint.

items.q: What gives life to the three pillars of empiricism?
items.back: The five Scrum Values.
items.analogy: The five Scrum Values (Commitment, Focus, Openness, Respect, Courage) create the team culture that makes transparency, inspection, and adaptation real. Values without pillars are platitudes; pillars without values are empty process.

items.q: Is there a "Sprint 0" in Scrum?
items.back: No. Sprints begin with Sprint 1 and an Increment must be attempted.
items.analogy: Sprint 0 is a waterfall concept smuggled into Scrum disguise — like calling your pre-trade research session a 'Trade 0'. Scrum starts with Sprint 1. If setup is needed, it's work — put it in the backlog and timebox it like any other Sprint.

items.q: True or False: A Scrum Team is cross-functional.
items.back: True. The team members have all the skills necessary to create value each Sprint.
items.analogy: True. The Scrum Team must collectively have all the skills needed to create a potentially releasable Increment every Sprint — no external dependencies on a 'DBA team' or 'network team' to get work Done.

items.q: Can the Product Owner order the Product Backlog based on risk or dependencies?
items.back: Yes. They can order it however they deem most appropriate to maximize value.
items.analogy: Yes. The PO has complete authority over Product Backlog ordering — by value, risk, learning, dependencies, or any other factor. They are the sole authority on what the team works on next.
